chapters.title: What an AI Agent Actually Is

blocks.robotComment: A chatbot answers one question. An agent decides what to do next — and then actually does it. 🔁
blocks.body: Every AI interaction covered so far in this app follows the same basic shape: you provide input, the model produces output, and that's it. An "agent" is something genuinely different — a system that can perceive a situation, decide what to do about it, and actually take action, often repeatedly, without a person handling every single step.

highlights.text: a system that can perceive a situation, decide what to do about it, and actually take action, often repeatedly, without a person handling every single step

blocks.body: That's the real difference: a plain chat response ends the moment it's produced — nothing happens as a result unless a person reads it and acts on it themselves. An agent can be the one that acts: checking a result, deciding a next step based on what it finds, and continuing until the actual goal is reached, not just until one reply is generated.

highlights.text: An agent can be the one that acts: checking a result, deciding a next step based on what it finds, and continuing until the actual goal is reached

blocks.body: This isn't a different kind of model under the hood — it's the same kind of language model this app has already covered, used in a different pattern: given a goal, a way to take actions, and a way to observe the results of those actions, then run in a loop instead of stopping after one response.

highlights.text: given a goal, a way to take actions, and a way to observe the results of those actions, then run in a loop instead of stopping after one response

blocks.question: What fundamentally distinguishes an AI agent from a plain single-response chat interaction?
options: An agent can perceive, decide, and act repeatedly toward a goal, instead of stopping after one reply
An agent uses a completely different, non-language-based kind of model
An agent can only ever produce text, never take any action
There is no real difference between the two at all
blocks.explanation: An agent's defining trait is acting repeatedly toward a goal — perceiving results and deciding next steps — rather than producing one reply and stopping.

blocks.sentence: A plain chat response ends the moment it's produced; an agent can keep going in a ___ until its actual goal is reached.
options: loop
database
spreadsheet
blocks.explanation: An agent's defining pattern is running in a loop — acting, observing results, and deciding the next step — rather than stopping after one output.

blocks.statement: An AI agent requires a fundamentally different, non-language-model technology than the chat interactions covered elsewhere in this app.
blocks.explanation: An agent typically uses the same kind of language model already covered in this app — the difference is the loop pattern it's used in, not the underlying model itself.

blocks.body: This isn't a brand-new idea to this app. Building With AI APIs already introduced function calling — a model requesting that your code run a described action and pass the result back — kept fully conceptual, with the request-and-response pattern as the whole focus.

highlights.text: Building With AI APIs already introduced function calling — a model requesting that your code run a described action and pass the result back

blocks.body: That earlier level covered the mechanical building block: how a single tool request and response actually works. This track goes further, into the decisions surrounding that mechanism — which tool to reach for, when to call it, how to judge whether the result actually moved toward the goal, and what to do next based on that judgment.

highlights.text: which tool to reach for, when to call it, how to judge whether the result actually moved toward the goal, and what to do next based on that judgment

blocks.body: Put simply: Building With AI APIs taught what a single tool call looks like. This track teaches what it takes to string many of them together, with real decisions in between, into something that can actually complete a multi-step task on its own.

highlights.text: Building With AI APIs taught what a single tool call looks like. This track teaches what it takes to string many of them together

blocks.body: Here's the full roadmap. Level 2 names the actual repeating cycle every agent runs on: perceive, decide, act. Level 3 goes deeper into tools specifically — not just that they exist, but how an agent decides which one to reach for and when.

highlights.text: Level 2 names the actual repeating cycle every agent runs on: perceive, decide, act

blocks.body: Levels 4 and 5 cover what makes multi-step behavior actually work: planning a goal out into steps ahead of time, and memory — what an agent keeps track of within a single run versus across separate runs.

highlights.text: planning a goal out into steps ahead of time, and memory — what an agent keeps track of within a single run versus across separate runs

L4-L5: What makes it work -> planning multi-step tasks, memory
L6-L7: Scaling up -> multiple agents working together, how much autonomy to grant

blocks.body: The second half scales up and turns practical: Level 6 covers multiple agents working together, Level 7 covers how much autonomy to actually grant an agent, and Levels 8-9 cover what happens when agents go wrong and how to design safe human oversight — which connects directly to the accountability questions this app's AI Ethics & Safety track covers. Level 10 ties the whole arc together.

blocks.robotComment: Before an agent can decide anything, it has to know what's actually going on. 👀
blocks.body: The loop this level names has three steps: perceive, decide, act. "Perceive" comes first — the agent looks at the current state of things, or the result of whatever action it just took, instead of working off a stale snapshot from when it started.

highlights.text: perceive, decide, act

blocks.body: What counts as "perceiving" depends on the task. A research agent perceives the search results it gets back. A scheduling agent perceives which calendar slots are actually free. A coding agent perceives whether a test passed or failed. In every case, it's reading the real, current state before deciding what to do about it.

highlights.text: it's reading the real, current state before deciding what to do about it

blocks.body: Perceiving isn't a one-time thing that happens only at the start. It happens every time the agent comes back around the loop, because the state can change between one cycle and the next — a search returns different results, a calendar slot gets booked, a test that failed now passes. Deciding based on an old, unchecked state is how an agent ends up acting on outdated information.

highlights.text: Deciding based on an old, unchecked state is how an agent ends up acting on outdated information

blocks.question: What does the "perceive" step of the agent loop actually involve?
options: Observing the current state of things, or the result of the last action, before deciding what to do next
Permanently fixing the agent's understanding of the world at the very start of a run
Choosing which tool to call
Writing a final summary of the whole run
blocks.explanation: Perceive means reading the current, real state — not working off a fixed starting snapshot.

blocks.sentence: An agent perceives the current state every time it comes back around the ___, not just once at the start.
options: loop
invoice
spreadsheet
blocks.explanation: Perceiving repeats on every cycle of the loop, since the state can change between cycles.

blocks.statement: Once an agent perceives the state at the very start of a run, it never needs to check it again.
blocks.explanation: The state can change between cycles, so an agent needs to perceive it again each time it loops back, not just once.

blocks.body: "Decide" is the middle step: choosing the next action based on the goal and whatever was just perceived. It's not a fixed script that runs the same way every time — the next action depends on what the agent actually found when it looked.

highlights.text: choosing the next action based on the goal and whatever was just perceived

blocks.body: Say a search comes back empty. A fixed script with no decision step would just move on to the next line, whether or not that still makes sense. An agent's decide step can instead choose to try a different search term, because that's what the current state actually calls for.

highlights.text: An agent's decide step can instead choose to try a different search term, because that's what the current state actually calls for

blocks.body: This is what separates an agent from plain automation: automation runs the same steps regardless of what happens along the way, while an agent's decisions branch based on what it perceives. That doesn't make the decision magic — it's still the same kind of reasoning covered elsewhere in this app, just applied fresh at every cycle instead of once.

highlights.text: automation runs the same steps regardless of what happens along the way, while an agent's decisions branch based on what it perceives

blocks.question: What makes the "decide" step different from a fixed automation script?
options: It chooses the next action based on the current state, so it can branch instead of always running the same steps
It always skips straight to the final action with no reasoning at all
It removes the need for a goal entirely
It only runs once, at the very beginning of a task
blocks.explanation: Deciding means choosing the next action based on what was just perceived, which lets an agent branch instead of following a fixed sequence.

blocks.sentence: A fixed automation script runs the same steps regardless of what happens; an agent's decisions ___ based on what it perceives.
options: branch
disappear
expire
blocks.explanation: The decide step lets an agent's next action change depending on the current state, rather than following one fixed path.

blocks.statement: The "decide" step in an agent loop always produces the exact same next action no matter what was just perceived.
blocks.explanation: Deciding is based on the current state, so the chosen action can change from one cycle to the next depending on what was perceived.

blocks.body: "Act" is the last of the three steps: actually carrying out the action that was just chosen, often through a tool call, rather than just describing what it would do. Deciding to check a calendar and actually checking it are two different things — act is where the second one happens.

highlights.text: actually carrying out the action that was just chosen, often through a tool call, rather than just describing what it would do

blocks.body: After acting, the agent doesn't stop. It goes back to perceive — but now the state has changed, because the action it just took produced a new result. That new result is the next thing to perceive, which is exactly what closes the loop: perceive, decide, act, then perceive again.

highlights.text: perceive, decide, act, then perceive again

blocks.code:
1. Perceive: check the current state or last result
2. Decide: choose the next action based on the goal and that state
3. Act: actually carry out the chosen action
4. Back to step 1, with a new state to perceive
blocks.caption: One full turn of the loop — and where it points right back to the start.

blocks.question: What happens immediately after the "act" step in the agent loop?
options: The agent goes back to perceiving, now with a new state produced by the action it just took
The task is always considered finished
The agent forgets the goal it was working toward
The loop restarts from a blank slate with no memory of what just happened
blocks.explanation: After acting, the agent loops back to perceive the new state that its action produced — that's what keeps the cycle going.

blocks.sentence: After acting, an agent loops back to perceive, decide, act, then ___ again.
options: perceive
invoice
delete
blocks.explanation: The loop closes by returning to perceive with the new state the last action produced.

blocks.statement: The "act" step means actually carrying out the chosen action, not just describing what the agent would do.
blocks.explanation: Acting means really taking the action, often via a tool call — not merely stating an intention.

Act, perceive, decide
Plan, execute, report

options: branch

options: perceive

questions.question: Why does perceiving happen on every cycle instead of just once?
options: Because the state can change between one cycle and the next
Because the goal changes on every cycle
Because tools cannot be reused
Because a model can only be asked one question ever

blocks.robotComment: One request, one response, done — that's not what this level is about. This is about what happens next. 🔁
blocks.body: Building With AI APIs covered a single request and response: you send one input, the model sends back one output, and that's the whole interaction. The perceive-decide-act loop is a genuinely different pattern — it keeps cycling instead of stopping after one exchange.

highlights.text: The perceive-decide-act loop is a genuinely different pattern — it keeps cycling instead of stopping after one exchange

blocks.body: In the loop, each cycle builds on the last: perceive the result of the previous action, decide the next step based on it, act, then perceive the new result. A single API call has no "previous action" to build on — it's one shot, and whatever happens next is up to whoever reads the response.

highlights.text: A single API call has no "previous action" to build on — it's one shot

blocks.body: That raises an obvious question: if the loop keeps cycling instead of stopping after one response, what makes it stop at all? A loop with no way to end would just keep running — so a real agent needs some condition that tells it the run is over, which is exactly what the rest of this level covers.

highlights.text: a real agent needs some condition that tells it the run is over

blocks.question: How does the perceive-decide-act loop differ from a single API call?
options: The loop keeps cycling, with each step building on the result of the last one, instead of stopping after one exchange
A single API call actually repeats forever, just like the loop does
The loop never involves a language model at all
There is no real difference between the two
blocks.explanation: A single API call is one request and one response; the loop keeps cycling, with each step building on the previous result.

blocks.sentence: A single API call is one request and one response; the agent loop keeps ___ instead of stopping after one exchange.
options: cycling
expiring
billing
blocks.explanation: The loop keeps going, cycle after cycle, rather than ending after a single request and response.

blocks.statement: A loop with no stopping condition at all would simply keep running indefinitely.
blocks.explanation: Without something telling it the run is over, a repeating loop has no natural point at which it would stop on its own.

blocks.body: The most natural way for the loop to end is the most obvious one: the goal is actually reached. The file is organized, the ticket is resolved, the email is sent and confirmed. Once that's true, there's nothing left to decide or act on, so the loop stops.

highlights.text: the goal is actually reached

blocks.body: Checking whether the goal is met happens during perceive: the agent looks at the current state and compares it against what the goal actually required. That comparison is what tells it whether to keep looping or stop — not a guess, and not just running out of steps to take.

highlights.text: the agent looks at the current state and compares it against what the goal actually required

blocks.body: This only works if the goal was actually checkable in the first place. "Organize this folder" is vague until it's turned into something an agent can verify — for example, every file sorted into a named subfolder. A goal that can't be checked against the state can't reliably tell the loop when to stop.

highlights.text: A goal that can't be checked against the state can't reliably tell the loop when to stop

blocks.question: How does an agent determine that the goal has been reached?
options: By comparing the current state, observed during perceive, against what the goal actually required
By counting how many actions it has taken so far, regardless of the result
By asking a person after every single action
It can never actually know whether the goal was reached
blocks.explanation: The perceive step is where the agent checks the current state against the goal, which is how it recognizes the goal has been met.

blocks.sentence: A goal that can't be ___ against the current state can't reliably tell the loop when to stop.
options: checked
invoiced
renamed
blocks.explanation: The goal needs to be something the agent can compare the state against, or it has no reliable way to know it's done.

blocks.statement: Reaching the goal is checked during the perceive step, by comparing the current state against what the goal required.
blocks.explanation: Perceiving the current state and comparing it to the goal is exactly how an agent recognizes that it's done.

blocks.body: Reaching the goal isn't the only valid reason for a loop to stop. A well-designed agent also stops when it hits a maximum number of steps or a time limit, when it runs into an error it can't resolve on its own, or when it reaches a point where handing off to a person makes more sense than continuing to guess.

highlights.text: when it hits a maximum number of steps or a time limit, when it runs into an error it can't resolve on its own, or when it reaches a point where handing off to a person makes more sense

blocks.body: These limits matter because a loop with no boundaries can get stuck: retrying the same failing action over and over, or drifting further from the goal with each cycle instead of closer to it. A step or time limit catches that even when the agent itself can't tell it's stuck.

highlights.text: retrying the same failing action over and over, or drifting further from the goal with each cycle instead of closer to it

blocks.body: So stopping conditions aren't a single rule — they're a small set of checks: did the goal get reached, did something fail in a way the agent can't handle, has it been going too long. Designing those checks is part of building the agent, not something to bolt on afterward.

highlights.text: Designing those checks is part of building the agent, not something to bolt on afterward

blocks.question: Besides reaching the goal, what is another valid reason for an agent loop to stop?
options: Hitting a step or time limit, or running into an error it can't resolve on its own
The agent randomly loses interest in the task
The loop should never stop for any reason other than reaching the goal
The model's training data runs out mid-task
blocks.explanation: Step limits, time limits, and unresolvable errors are all legitimate reasons for a loop to stop besides reaching the goal.

blocks.sentence: Without a step or time limit, a stuck agent could keep retrying the same failing action ___.
options: indefinitely
briefly
accidentally
blocks.explanation: A loop with no boundaries can keep repeating a failing action or drifting from the goal with no natural end point.

blocks.statement: Designing stopping conditions is something that should be built into an agent from the start, not added as an afterthought.
blocks.explanation: Stopping conditions like step limits, time limits, and error handling are part of designing the agent itself.
